name: Poiseuille's law
seoDesc: Poiseuille's law: work out radius of the pipe (r) from the dynamic viscosity and the pressure change. A free physics calculator with the formula, units…
summary: Give the Poiseuille's law calculator the dynamic viscosity, the pressure change, the volumetric flow rate and the resistance and it returns radius of the pipe (r). That makes it useful for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Poiseuille's law calculator work?
sections.html:
The Poiseuille's law calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports radius of the pipe (r) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the dynamic viscosity (μ), the pressure change (Δp), the volumetric flow rate (Q) and the resistance (R).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Poiseuille's law calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Radius of the pipe (r)=(2 ^ 3 ÷ 4) × (volumetric flow rate (Q) × length of the pipe (l) × dynamic viscosity (μ) ÷ pressure change (Δp) ^ 1 ÷ 4) ÷ (PI ^ 1 ÷ 4)
Length of the pipe (l)=(1 ÷ 8) × PI × (radius of the pipe (r) ^ 4) × resistance (R) ÷ dynamic viscosity (μ)
End pressure=initial pressure − pressure change (Δp)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Viscosity – dynamic, opening in pascal seconds
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Pressure, opening in pascals
  • Volume, opening in cubic meters
  • Viscosity – dynamic, opening in pascal seconds
  • Pressure, opening in pascals
  • Pressure, opening in pascals

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Poiseuille's law calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the dynamic viscosity, the pressure change and the volumetric flow rate — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Poiseuille's law calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns radius of the pipe (r), derived from the dynamic viscosity, the pressure change and the volumetric flow rate. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Poiseuille's law calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the dynamic viscosity, the pressure change, the volumetric flow rate and the resistance, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter dynamic viscosity (μ) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Dynamic viscosity (μ) opens in pascal seconds and the chip beside it offers 11 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: Is the Poiseuille's law calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
